lines: One source just stops talking for a while.
Nothing crashed. Nothing errored. It simply has nothing new to say.
And somehow, that alone is enough to freeze everything downstream of it.
There's when something actually happened, out in the world.
And there's when your own system finally gets around to noticing it.
Those two can drift apart by a little, or by a lot, with nothing forcing them back together.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A claim gets made: nothing older than this point is still coming.
Can a real system actually promise that, and mean it every single time?
answer: For almost any real, spread-out source, there's simply no way to be certain nothing older is still on its way.
So the claim ends up being an educated guess, not a promise.

lines: That guess, in most real systems, is exactly what it has to be: a guess, not a fact.
And it isn't made once for the whole system. Each piece makes its own guess, separately.
Which means the overall answer is only ever as current as whichever piece has said the least.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
One of those pieces just goes quiet and stays quiet, with nothing explicitly watching for it.
Does the overall answer eventually move past it anyway, or does it just wait forever?
answer: It waits forever, which is exactly the trap.
Nothing automatically notices that silence means silence, rather than simply more data still to come.
Somebody has to actually decide, on purpose, how long is too long to wait.

lines: Decide that, on purpose, and the quiet one gets politely written off.
Everyone else's progress counts again, instead of being held hostage to one gone-quiet voice.
The whole thing starts moving again, the moment that decision actually gets made.
There's a mirror version of this same problem, running the opposite direction entirely.
One piece races way out ahead of the rest, and whoever's listening has to hold onto everything it sends.
Rein that one in instead, and nobody downstream has to hoard nearly as much.
Pull that claim in tighter, and you hear back sooner — at the cost of getting some of it wrong the first time.
Loosen it instead, and you wait longer, but what you hear back is far more likely to already be right.
Neither one of those is simply the better choice. It depends entirely on what you actually need.
Every figure in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy models.
The freeze that really happened, and the fix that really thawed it back out.
And the trade-off itself, not asserted, but actually measured both ways.
So: two separate clocks, free to drift apart, with nothing forcing them back together.
A claim of completeness that's honest about being a guess, not a promise.
And a dial that always trades one thing for the other, in whichever direction you actually need it to.
